name: Internal monitoring and minimum-revenue quotas drive concurrent employment and continuous identity acquisition

attribution.legal_posture: BBC first-person historical testimony, corroborated only in broad outline; defensive synthesis of cited public sources; technique mapping describes methods rather than an identity; universal rate estimate status is unreported.

caveats: ATT&CK references describe analogous observable behavior; employer-system use for DPRK internal surveillance requires source-specific evidence.
BBC could not independently verify every specific in the testimony, although another former-worker account and a separate defector supported the general description.
False-positive caution: Behavior may reflect labor exploitation or coercion. Preserve worker safety and legal obligations rather than treating every case solely as malicious insider conduct.
Many people lawfully hold multiple jobs or work flexible hours. Productivity metrics are error-prone and unsuitable for broad employee surveillance.
Jin-su is a source-protection pseudonym and must remain context-only.
The 85 percent figure comes from one former worker's historical account; a current program-wide rate requires broader data.
The protected BBC pseudonym Jin-su remains source context; it carries only the source's protected label.

statements: The BBC's pseudonymous former worker said his China-based group generally worked in teams of ten and that he remitted 85 percent of earnings to the state-linked system.
He described holding multiple jobs across the United States and Europe and earning at least about $5,000 per month, while some colleagues earned more.

BBC reports 24-hour screen monitoring, sanctions for sustained underperformance, rising monthly revenue targets, and workers holding three or four company roles to meet quotas. UN S/2020/151 independently reports a minimum-earnings rule and removal for prolonged failure. Together they support a control mechanism that explains job volume and persona churn without converting those behaviors into standalone attribution signals.
